newsitem.title: USA: Israel won't pick up Syria talks where they ended.
newsitem.headline: Israel won't pick up Syria talks where they ended.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday rejected Syrian demands to pick up peace talks at the point where they left off and accused Damascus of blocking Israel's desire to withdraw from Lebanon.

"Obviously we will take note of what took place in the talks between Syrian negotiators and the previous (Israeli) government," Netanyahu said in a speech to the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, a private think-tank.
But, he added, "we cannot be bound by conversations or by ideas or by speculations and suggestions and hypotheses. We can only honour signed agreements."

Syria says Israel's former Labour government agreed to withdraw in full from the Golan Heights, the main point of contention in the five-year-old talks. But Netanyahu's Likud government is against such a withdrawal.
Labour broke off peace talks almost a year ago after a series of bomb blasts in Israel, and they have not resumed.
An Israeli official said that discussions on Thursday between Netanyahu and U.S. President Bill Clinton achieved no breakthrough in efforts to resume peace talks with Syria.

That assessment by Israeli Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh, who accompanied Netanyahu here and was speaking to Israel Radio, contrasted with a more optimistic statement by Clinton that he was hopeful talks would restart.

Netanyahu said he was "still puzzled" by Syria's refusal to discuss an Israeli withdrawal from South Lebanon in return for an end to attacks on Israel by Lebanese Hizbollah guerrillas who operate with tacit Syrian approval.
"I am saying that we want to withdraw from Lebanon ... but I am being told in the Syrian press: don't withdraw from Lebanon. Now Syria ostensibly seeks our withdrawal but in practice impedes it."
Middle East diplomats say Syria sees the Hizbollah attacks as leverage in the Golan dispute. Syria has rejected Israeli proposals to discuss Lebanon before dealing with the Golan.

Netanyahu said that if Syrian President Hafez al-Assad decided to "choose the path of peace" he would find the Israelis "reasonable and cooperative partners". He gave no details of what Israeli officials said was a formula he had brought to Washington for restarting the talks.
Netanyahu gave no sign of Israeli flexibility in talks with the Palestinians due to resume next month to decide the "final status" of Palestinian self-rule areas.
He said Jerusalem, one of the points at issue, "will continue to be undivided and under our sovereignty."
Palestinian demands for a state covering the whole of the occupied territories and East Jerusalem would lead to a breakdown in the talks, he said.
He also said Israel was "certainly going to develop" existing Jewish settlements in the occupied territories, although it had not decided on new ones.

Netanyahu dwelt at length on what he said was the lack of "education for peace" in the Arab world, charging that Arab children were still not being taught to accept Israel as a permanent part of the Middle East landscape.

Earlier, in an appearance on NBC television, Netanyahu said he could not confirm a report in the Washington Post Thursday that Israel had known since 1994 about the Jewish ancestry of U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.
Recent revelations that the Czech-born Albright, who was raised a Roman Catholic, had three Jewish grandparents who died in the Holocaust have caused a sensation in Washington.

"If the late prime minister (Yitzhak) Rabin knew about it, he didn't confide it to me," Netanyahu said. He added drily: "Not that it makes any difference. We don't hold anything against anyone being Jewish, you know."
